title: Cluster primitive interop and output guidelines
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures design guidance for the set of Terraform primitives we maintain for Private Deployments: network (VPC/subnets/route tables), IAM primitives (roles/policies/assumable principals), and cluster primitives (EKS/GKE/AKS minimal surface). The goal is to define module boundaries, stable outputs, variable conventions, and an upgrade/migration playbook so consumers (Dedicated, Private, and partner installs) can upgrade reliably with minimal tfstate surgery.

Audience:
- Infra module maintainers
- Solutions engineers executing Private installs
- SRE/Platform teams who run upgrades in customer environments

Key design principles (short):
- Small, single-purpose primitives: vpc-primitive, iam-primitive, cluster-primitive-cloud-specific (eks-primitive, gke-primitive, aks-primitive). Keep each module focused on one provider surface.
- Stable outputs: outputs are the public contract. Add new outputs permissively; never rename or remove outputs unless part of a major migration with tooling to rewrite state.
- Variables: prefer explicit inputs over magic detection. Use "map"/"object" minimally; prefer flat variables with clear prefixes for cross-cloud mapping.
- Idempotent upgrades: upgrades should be achievable via terraform plan + apply with no manual state edits for minor/patch bumps. When state edits are required, document exact terraform state mv steps.

Module boundaries and responsibilities:
- vpc-primitive: create VPC, subnets (private/app, private/db, nat), route tables, IGW if needed, TGW attachments left out (higher-level). Expose subnet ids, route table ids, nat eips, and cidr blocks as outputs.
- iam-primitive: create named roles and policies that are minimal and assumable. Output role ARNs and policy ARNs and also the role name. Avoid embedding account ids in role names; accept account_id as an input for edge cases.
- eks/gke/aks primitives: focus on cluster resource itself and node pool attachment primitives. Do NOT try to manage higher-level addons (ingress controllers, cert-manager) from primitives; instead expose endpoints and CA data.

Output naming conventions (contract):
- Prefix outputs with the module logical name, e.g., vpc_id, vpc_private_subnet_ids, vpc_public_route_table_id. Keep names explicit and predictable.
- For cluster modules: cluster_endpoint, cluster_certificate_authority_data, cluster_name, cluster_version, cluster_node_role_arn(s).
- For IAM: role_arn, role_name, inline_policy_ids (if created).
- Always include a string-formatted id and a list-of-strings variant for collections: e.g., subnet_ids (list) and subnet_id_primary (string) if a canonical one exists.

Variable conventions:
- Conventional prefixes: vpc_, iam_, cluster_. E.g., vpc_cidr_block, iam_assume_principals, cluster_kubernetes_version.
- Minimal machine-friendly defaults: avoid hardcoding AZ choices; accept a list of availability_zones. Default counts minimal (node_count = 1) but require overrides in production.
- Provider versions should be pinned by consumers; modules should document recommended provider versions in README but not force them via terraform required_providers (to ease reuse across workspaces).

Cross-cloud abstraction guidance:
- Do not create heavy abstraction that tries to normalize every cloud field. Provide a thin mapping layer at the platform level (higher-level module) that composes cloud-specific primitives. Keep primitives thin and cloud-aligned.
- Shared naming: where possible use the same logical output names across cloud primitives (cluster_endpoint, cluster_ca, cluster_name) so higher-level code can be cloud-agnostic.

State and upgrade playbook (summary):
1) Preparation: document current module version in the cluster workspace (tfstate). Capture plan baseline: terraform plan -out before upgrade.
2) Read release notes for new module (breaking changes section). If no breaking changes, do terraform init -upgrade and terraform apply.
3) For minor breaking changes (output renames, moved resources): perform a dry-run with terraform state mv instructions recorded. Example: terraform state mv module.old_vpc.aws_vpc.this[0] module.new_vpc.aws_vpc.this[0] followed by plan/apply.
4) For major semantic changes (resource model rework) follow staged migration: create shadow-module (vN) in parallel with vN+1, import resources into new module using terraform import or state mv, validate outputs, cut over by adjusting root module to reference new module instances.
5) Rollback: keep the pre-upgrade state snapshot file; if apply causes bad drift, restore state and rollback module reference in code.

Concrete upgrade steps for an output rename example:
- Before: old module exported vpc_subnet_ids
- After: new module exports vpc_private_subnet_ids and vpc_public_subnet_ids
Steps:
  a) Plan: git branch that updates module source to v2 and keep old module code as module.old
  b) terraform init -upgrade
  c) terraform plan -out plan.tfplan (inspect changes)
  d) If resources unchanged but outputs renamed, do
     terraform state mv module.old.aws_subnet.private[0] module.new.aws_subnet.private[0]
  e) Apply and validate higher-level resources that consumed the outputs (LBs, node groups).

Testing and validation checklist (pre-apply):
- Static checks: run tflint, terraform validate against the root module.
- Integration dry-run: terraform plan produced and stored; inspect any resource replacements.
- Smoke tests: after apply, run: curl cluster_endpoint/health, kubectl get nodes, ensure node count and taints are expected.
- IAM tests: verify role can be assumed from the service account or CI principal.

On‑prem variant notes (air-gapped/VPC-lite):
- For on-prem we cannot rely on cloud provider resources. Provide a shim module that implements the same output contract but sources values from inputs (e.g., onprem_vpc_id input, onprem_subnet_ids). This lets platform code treat on-prem as a first-class citizen without major changes.
- Document the differences clearly: no IGW, no NAT EIPs. Node pools are often VM groups managed outside Terraform; expose placeholders and clear guidance for operators.

Provider and tooling recommendations:
- Recommended provider versions listed in module README, e.g., aws >= 4.40, kubernetes >= 2.11. Pin CI pipelines to those versions.
- Use terraform 1.4+ in CI for stable provider dependency handling.
- Provide helper scripts under /scripts/upgrade to automate state mv sequences for common patterns.

Compatibility matrix (summary):
- v1.x (current): minimal contract, exposes vpc_id, subnet_ids, role_arn, cluster_endpoint.
- v2.x (target): split subnet outputs, node role separation, better tagging. Backwards compatible if consumers use vpc_id and subnet_ids; not compatible if consumers rely on specific naming.
- Migration complexity: low -> moderate depending on consumer coupling.

Rollout strategy for customer environments:
- Canary: select a single low-risk workspace, run the upgrade, confirm telemetry and smoke tests.
- Gradual rollout: move groups of workspaces clustered by region/account.
- Full roll: after 2-3 canaries with no regressions and resolved edge-cases.

IAM policy evolution guidance:
- Avoid embedding broad permissions in default policies. Start with least-privilege and surface a small policy snippet consumers can append to handle edge operations.
- When changing a role name/ARN, prefer creating a new role and marking the old one deprecated for one release cycle, then remove. Provide a conversion guide: how to update trust relationships for service accounts.

Example variables and outputs (canonical example to copy into module README):
- variables.tf snippet (string):
  variable "vpc_cidr_block" { description = "Primary CIDR" type = string default = "10.0.0.0/16" }
  variable "availability_zones" { description = "list of AZs to use" type = list(string) default = ["us-west-2a", "us-west-2b"] }

- outputs.tf snippet (string):
  output "vpc_id" { description = "ID of created VPC" value = aws_vpc.this.id }
  output "vpc_private_subnet_ids" { description = "Private subnet ids" value = aws_subnet.private.*.id }

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How aggressively should primitives enforce tags and naming conventions vs leaving that to higher level modules? Proposal: primitives require a minimal set of tags (owner, environment) but not business-specific tags.
- Should we introduce a thin shim library (Go/Python) that can rewrite tfstate for common rename patterns? Feels useful for complex customer upgrades.
- Confirm on-prem shim interface shape with Solutions Engineering before publishing final version.

Next steps:
- Share this draft with infra module owners and Solutions Eng (CC: Marco, Lena, Diego) for feedback by 2025-11-09.
- Create a repository folder: infra-modules/upgrade-guides/ with automated state-mv scripts for the top 5 upgrade patterns.
- Schedule a 90-minute working session to align on output names and the on-prem shim interface.

Notes to self (working):
- Keep the primitives tiny; anything that needs multi-resource orchestration belongs at the platform composition layer.
- Document exact terraform state commands when proposing breaking output renames. People will copy/paste them during upgrades.
